title: Savory Cocktails Are Having a Moment. Here Are 23 to Try.
summary:
If you like your martinis with more olive brine than vodka, you’ll love these savory cocktails.

The post Savory Cocktails Are Having a Moment. Here Are 23 to Try. appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
As we mature as drinkers, our palates evolve. That’s why, much like a favorite childhood candy, sweet concoctions may not hit the same way over time. They may taste more cloying or lacking in complexity, leaving us wondering what else is out there. Enter savory cocktails, which call on flavors from fish sauce to chili bitters to challenge palates and offer delicious alternatives to sugar-forward drinks. Bars across the country are getting in on the trend, introducing new offerings that go far beyond olive juice-splashed dirty martinis.

In recent years, pickles have taken the internet by storm in the form of martinis, shots, and Sauvignon Blanc. Dirty martinis have even made the jump from drinks to food, inspiring everything from a briny salad dressing to an olive-studded pasta. It points to the wider embrace of savory cocktail flavors, particularly in combinations outside the norm.

“I’ve noticed a larger trend of people asking for traditional cocktails to be less sweet,” says bartender Emily Holser, adding that she believes this can be a gateway to expanding one’s palate.

Interested in finding a savory cocktail that speaks to you? For all of the umami lovers out there, here are some of Wine Enthusiast’s favorite savory libations, from an everything bagel-inspired martini to a jerk spice daiquiri.

The Classics

Dirty Martini

Forget sugary Appletinis and fruit juice-spiked Mississippi bourbon punch. If your drink preferences skew more savory than sweet, the dirty martini belongs in your order queue. With a deep umami kick from a heavy-handed splash of salty olive brine, this cocktail has earned its honored spot in the cocktail canon.

Spicy Margarita

Whether you’re a lifelong spice fiend or simply looking to heat up your next happy hour, consider the spicy margarita. With cucumber and jalapeño, this recipe brings a savory punch to the classic agave cocktail.

Bloody Mary

With ingredients such as horseradish, tomato juice, and hot sauce, the Bloody Mary might be one of the most polarizing classic cocktails. If you’re a die-hard fan, add a few drops of Worcestershire sauce.

Traditional Michelada

If your guests crave a savory hop-tail, try this Mexican classic. The michelada melds a Bloody Mary with Mexican light-style ale, while its salted rim gives a small nod to the country’s other signature drink: the margarita.

Adventurous Riffs

Dirty Spritz

Originating from viral bouts around social media, the Dirty Spritz is well on its way to classic cocktail status. Drinkers love this lower-abv twist on a dirty martini that combines sparkling wine, olive brine, and sherry.

Pickle Martini

Dirty martini lovers, we present to you: the pickle martini. This salty riff takes the classic one step further with the addition of pickle brine, while aquavit adds an herbal touch.

Tomatini

Tomato cocktails have been making their way onto more and more menus in recent years with varying degrees of complexity. This tomatini recipe takes a simpler route by muddling a tomato with white balsamic vinegar, vodka, salt, and black pepper.

Jerk Daiquiri

Classic jerk seasoning highlights flavors such as hot peppers, thyme, and allspice. This jerk daiquiri infuses those flavors into the classic cocktail with a combination of thyme simple syrup, habanero smoked saline solution, and St. Elizabeth Allspice Dram.

Dill Breaker

While dill in a cocktail might have sounded insane a decade ago, it’s become much more palatable to modern tastes as savory cocktails have made their way mainstream. The Dill Breaker, which blends dill cordial with vodka and lemon juice, is actually one of the tamer drinks on this list.

Everything Bagel Martini

Building off classic dirty martini ingredients, this everything bagel martini just makes sense. Everything bagel spice delivers rich umami flavor and an appealingly crunchy texture—it’s our new favorite thing to put on a martini rim.

Mexican Martini

What do you get when you cross a dirty martini with a margarita? A Mexican martini, of course. Olive brine meets classic margarita ingredients in this savory riff, served up. If you want to add a salt rim, we wouldn’t be mad.

Smoky Mary

If you want to take your Bloody Mary to the next level, try the Smoky Mary. Mezcal imparts a savory, smoky note to the classic brunch cocktail.

Pickle Shot

This strong-and-sour pickle shooter has been making the rounds on social media for the past couple of years. We can see why: It’s a fun, playful drink that’s easy to make and adapts to whichever ingredients are in your bar/kitchen.

Crazy Concoctions

Chicken Soup Martini

Don’t worry, this chicken soup martini doesn’t actually contain any poultry. Rather, it relies on a combination of olive brine and a mirepoix infusion to channel all the savory, umami flavors.

Tomato-Anchovy Martini

Want to mix up something even crazier than a tomatini? Check out the tomato-anchovy martini. This drink uses Veso’s Anchovy Vermouth for a saline touch that isn’t too overpowering.

Parmesan Espresso Martini

Behold the parmesan espresso martini—which is exactly what it sounds like and better than you’d expect. The parmesan-infused vodka and thin layer of grated cheese make a delightfully smooth and savory cocktail.

Celine-Dijon

File this under unlikely combinations that somehow just work. The pun-tastic Celine-Dijon, which gets its punch from Dijon mustard and passionfruit, makes our heart go on.

Latke Sour

With a spuds-forward flavor, rich froth, and a whiff of smokiness, the Latke Sour is practically a potato pancake in drink form.

Seven Serpents

Taking inspiration from the Aztec goddess of corn and sustenance, Chicomecóatl, the Seven Serpents is a spicy corn cocktail featuring chili bitters, fresh corn juice, lemon juice, and the spirit of your choice.

Smoke on the Water

Yes, making the nori-infused gin for the Smoke on the Water requires a little bit of planning, but once that’s done, it’s smooth sailing ahead. The addition of white port and Talisker make up this smoky yet salty cocktail.

Sober Sippers

Non-Alcoholic Bloody Mary

One could argue that this non-alcoholic Bloody Mary is just gazpacho in a glass, but we like to think this batched mocktail is more than that. If you want to truly distinguish it, add your favorite NA spirit.

Non-Alcoholic Michelada

This NA Michelada is perfect when entertaining teetotalers and drinkers alike. Simply prepare the savory accouterments and crack open a variety of alcoholic and non-alcoholic light beers.

Carrot Mocktail

With fresh orange juice and zero-proof tequila, this savory and sophisticated mocktail is worth sipping all year long.

title: This Internet-Famous Korean Coffee Drink Is Even Better as a Cocktail
summary:
With rum, Frangelico, and coconut soju, the Dalgona cocktail is a delightful sweet treat.

The post This Internet-Famous Korean Coffee Drink Is Even Better as a Cocktail appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
First, there was dalgona candy, a traditional Korean confection with flavors some liken to honeycomb or butterscotch; the word “dalgona” comes from the Korean word for “sweet.

Then came dalgona coffee, a popular Korean coffee drink that went viral on social media in 2020. It seemed like everyone was vigorously mixing instant coffee, sugar, and hot water until thick, caramel-colored peaks emerged. The fluffy, toffee-like cloud was then spooned atop milk for a sweet, drinkable treat.

This next creative evolution is a mash-up of dalgona coffee and the espresso martini, courtesy of Haera Shin, the beverage director for Momofuku, David Chang’s restaurant group. A native New Yorker with Korean heritage, Shin was inspired by the series Squid Game to make this playful riff, which was on the menu at the Netflix Bites pop-up restaurant in Las Vegas. The recipe is also featured in her new book, Korean Cocktails: From Traditional Spirits to Modern Drinks.

“In the first season [of Squid Game], one of the challenges involves carving out a shape from a dalgona candy,” she recalls. The South Korean survival drama debuted in 2021—right around the height of the global dalgona coffee craze.

Instead of vodka, flavored soju adds a focused burst of coconut flavor alongside rum, while a frothy Korean coffee whip evokes the popular caffeinated quaff.

“Don’t worry,” Shin assures. “No deadly consequences if you fail this challenge!”

Dalgona

Courtesy of Korean Cocktails: From Traditional Spirits to Modern Drinks by Haera Shin (Countryman Press, 2026)

Ingredients

1 ½ ounces Planteray Rum 3 Stars (or other preferred white rum)
¾ ounce Frangelico
½ ounce coconut soju
2 ounces oat milk
½ ounce honey syrup (1:1 honey to water)
Whipped Korean coffee, to top*

Directions

Combine all ingredients except whipped coffee in a cocktail shaker with ice. Shake vigorously, then strain into a snifter filled with ice. Spoon whipped coffee on top.

*To make whipped Korean coffee: Combine ¼ cup instant coffee, ¼ cup boiling water, and ¼ cup sugar in a medium bowl. Whip together with a handheld mixer until light and fluffy, with medium-stiff peaks. Store in a container in the refrigerator until ready to use, for up to one day. Makes ½ cup whipped cream (enough for 2 drinks).

title: A Promising New AVA Is Gaining Traction in the South
summary:
Despite just being established in 2025, North Carolina’s Tryon Foothills AVA is already making a name for itself.

The post A Promising New AVA Is Gaining Traction in the South appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Michael Myers, the executive beverage director for Charlotte, North Carolina’s Irreverently Refined hospitality group, knows a lot about wine. But when he needed to find local wines for a special North Carolina-themed menu at one of his restaurants, he wasn’t sure where to look.

“North Carolina wines weren’t really on our list,” Myers says. “We had maybe used one or two. And it kind of started as a joke: ‘What are we going to use for North Carolina wine?’ No one wanted to force it and just use North Carolina wines because we had to.”

But when Myers tasted a couple of wines from the nearby Tryon Foothills AVA, about 90 minutes west of Charlotte, he changed his mind.

“It was one of the most humbling things for me as a wine person that I didn’t know about these wines,” he says. “They were in my backyard.”

In many of the United States’s smaller, less-known American Viticultural Areas—and especially those that aren’t on the West Coast—this isn’t unusual. In North Carolina, the conversation usually begins and ends with the 150,000-case winery at the historic Biltmore Estate in Asheville.

YEAR AVA ESTABLISHED: 2025
TOTAL ACREAGE: 112,512
PLANTED ACREAGE: 50
NUMBER OF WINERIES: 4 ELEVATION RANGE: 712 to 1,656 feet

In this case, though, Tryon Foothills, despite being one of the country’s newest AVAs and having only a handful of wineries, has garnered more attention than its youth and production size would seem to warrant.

“We use it as a talking point, as a teaching point, about what can be done with an AVA,” says Nicole Chesney, the executive director of the North Carolina Wine & Grape Council. “It’s really been fun to see what has been done in the AVA.”

The Tryon Foothills AVA was only established in September 2025, but grape cultivation in the area dates back at least 150 years, including Muscadines. The region sits on the eastern foothills of the Blue Ridge Mountains, reaching elevations of up to 1,600 feet. That accounts for the unique feature in its terroir that justified the creation of the AVA—a “thermal belt,” where warm air remains on the slopes while cooler air drains to the valley floors below, creating a grape-growing environment that is much different from elsewhere in the state.

Tryon Hills doesn’t have the humidity or heat problems found elsewhere in North Carolina that require growers to focus on hybrid grapes. Rather, it allows them to work with more vinifera, like Merlot and Petit Verdot, says Cory Lillberg, the vineyard manager at Parker-Binns Vineyard. He was also the driving force behind the AVA petition, which had been lingering for almost two decades.

Lillberg says vinifera in the Tryon Foothills can ripen and hang longer, resulting in higher alcohol levels and wines that are richer and fruitier than those from other parts of the state and across much of the East Coast.

“The geologic conditions really give us a style and expression that’s different,” says Lillberg, whose winery makes between 3,000 and 5,000 cases a year.

The next goal? To attract more wineries and growers to take advantage of that unique terroir—which Lillberg hopes the new AVA will help accomplish.

MOST WIDELY PLANTED GRAPES: Merlot, Petit Verdot, Vidal Blanc, Petit Manseng
CLIMATE: Moderate, with an occasional early frost
SOIL TYPES: Rocky, clay, and loam

Bet You Didn’t Know

From the late 19th century until World War II, Tryon’s Rockhouse Winery shipped its grapes—primarily Niagara and Delaware—around the U.S., and “Tryon and grapes were synonymous like Milwaukee and beer,” according to the book Tryon Memories by Elizabeth Doubleday Frost.

content:
The Dinner Party Is Dead. Let’s Have a Séance.

Those who feed the village also get to build it.

I cannot stop thinking about a recent article from The Atlantic titled “Why Americans Stopped Throwing Dinner Parties.” The statistics are staggering. From 1975 to 2026, the percentage of Americans who host friends or family at least once a month dropped from 42% to 12%. That’s a 70% decline in just over 50 years.

This cliff-like drop isn’t simply because people are going out more. Rather, it’s because eating and being alone is the easiest it’s ever been. .

People collectively say they want more time spent with their community, socializing, and being together. But when it comes to actually making it happen, gathering becomes another daunting task, one so easily avoided by staying home and scrolling through our personalized feeds.

It reminds me of an expression I keep seeing on social media, especially in conversations about parenting and community: Everyone wants a village, but nobody wants to be a villager.

As a busy parent living in a small community, I resonate with this sentiment deeply. And perhaps nowhere is it felt more acutely than among parents of young children. The Atlantic article cites how much more time parents spend with their kids than at any other point in recent history. We’re more involved, more scheduled, and more exhausted with family life, and with that more isolated from our larger support networks.

But here’s the thing about a village: It doesn’t build itself. Someone has to invite the townspeople over. Someone has to put food on the table. Someone has to be willing to make the effort, even when it’s inconvenient.

Of course there’s the argument that hosting is a luxury. And sure, it can be. But I can tell you firsthand that the bar is so low these days, simply letting people into your home and putting out whatever leftovers, random snacks, or open bottle of wine is in your fridge is more than enough. 

My grandma, a devoted student of the Depression era, living off practically nothing, used to always say, “Even if we only have tuna fish, at least we will be together.” That’s the sentiment we need to bring back. And I think the wine world is just the community to do it.

I’m not saying that simply because wine itself is the ultimate vehicle for gathering. I’m talking about the art of hospitality. The instinct to welcome people in, make them comfortable, feed them, pour them something delicious, and create an experience to remember, regardless of how much or little time it takes to prepare.

Social media hasn’t just forced us all into splintered isolation. It’s also raised the expectations of what it means to host. Every dinner party seems to require an impossibly beautiful tablesetting, elaborate menu, perfect lighting, and flowers that look like they were arranged by a professional. This barrier to entry is terrifying to newbies. I consider myself a very experienced host and even I can’t meet those expectations. 

But a dinner party doesn’t need to be a production to be meaningful.

When was the last time someone cooked dinner for you in their home? Really think about it. While I have high standards for my own cooking, even when I’ve just assembled what’s around to share, I have never had someone not be grateful. I often find myself throwing together a simple snack platter–olives, nuts, great butter with hunks of bread. Or if you’re feeling ambitious, some homemade hummus or this house-favorite scallion yogurt dip. The act itself feels more scarce than ever.

And let me tell you, as someone who’s become a very practiced host, the effort—no matter how large or small—will always pay you back in spades.

I’ve built new friendships, forged relationships, heard incredible gossip, and ended countless nights dancing in my kitchen while doing the dishes to early 2000s pop-punk. Was I tired the next day? Of course. But I’m tired all the time. I have two young kids and a demanding full time job, just like everyone else.

Yet, there’s something wonderful about that sleepy glow of exhaustion after a night spent bringing people together. It’s the kind of tiredness that feels like you actually did something worthwhile with your life.

We can’t keep wishing for deeper friendships, stronger neighborhoods, and a greater sense of belonging while waiting for someone else to organize it all. Being a good villager means showing up for other people. And in my opinion, being a host is a huge part of that.

Inconvenience is the cost of community. 

Which brings me back to the wine community.

We are surrounded by people who understand the magic of gathering around a table. People who know that a bottle of wine tastes better when it’s shared, that food doesn’t need to be fancy to be memorable, and that hospitality is about how you make people feel, not how impressive your house looks. You know the junk drawer? I have junk tablescapes. 

We have the knowledge, the instincts, and the passion to make hosting feel accessible again. So why aren’t we teaching more people how to do it?

Here’s my conch call to all the hospitality folks out there in the wine community: We need you more than ever.

Help me bring back the dinner party. Even a lingering lunch will do. Not the intimidating, Instagram-perfect version. The real one. The one where the kitchen sink is full of dishes, someone’s sitting next to a cutting board on the counter, the food is simple, and nobody wants to leave. 

Let’s teach people how to host without making it a monumental undertaking. Dinner Party 101. The absolute laziest way to throw a great party. What to cook, what to pour, what to skip, and how to stop worrying about whether everything is perfect.

This is why we launched a Home & Entertaining section of the site dedicated to highlighting all the ways people gather, including how well-known hosts like Vin et Hip Hop founder Jermaine Stone and lifestyle influencer Chloe Crane-Leroux throw a party, to wine recommendations for hosting a low-key girls night in.

Because everyone wants a village. It’s time we all started acting like villagers. And if all we have is tuna fish and a bottle of wine, at least we’ll be together. I’ll bring the can opener and the corkscrew. 

Send me your best ideas, shortcuts, and hosting tricks, and I’ll start sharing them. Email me at jstrum@wineenthusiast.com or DM me @jackistrum. 

Jacqueline Strum

President & Publisher of Wine Enthusiast Media

title: Livermore Valley, American Wine Region of the Year, Is Making Wine Joyful
summary:
The Livermore Valley has always been one of the hallmark regions for winemaking in Northern California. But its collaborative spirit is fueling an even brighter future.

The post Livermore Valley, American Wine Region of the Year, Is Making Wine Joyful appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Livermore Valley, California, is being recognized as Wine Enthusiast’s 2026 American Wine Region of the Year. But what makes this year different from any other?

The Livermore Valley has always been one of the hallmark regions for grape-growing and winemaking in Northern California. In addition to winning the Grand Prize at the Paris Exposition in 1889, it’s responsible for one of the most phenomenal clonal selections of all time: the Wente Clone, which is used to make Chardonnay all over the world. 

Known for signature expressions of Sauvignon Blanc and Cabernet Franc, long-standing, multi-generational wineries (like Wente Family Vineyards and Concannon Vineyard) have continued to propel the region forward, while small family operations are experimenting with lesser-used varietals, like Torrontés and Timorasso. 

The Livermore Valley Wine Community has been run by Executive Director Brandi Lombardi for 19 years, and is the headquarters of the nearly two-year-old Global Artisan Vintners Alliance. The Global AVA is comprised of 12 wine regions around the world, including Livermore, and focuses on creating a “thriving and inclusive global wine economy that strengthens locally owned and operated wineries and fosters enhanced agritourism in lesser-known wine regions.”

In addition to tech-fueled population growth in the region, there has been a recent explosion of thoughtful wine events, including TASTE: The Livermore Valley Wine Experience, Terroir at the Table, and Cab Franc-A-Palooza.

The region also has one of the highest percentages of women winemakers in the United States. The region’s mission has always reflected the Livermore Valley Wine Community’s tagline: “Wine tasting as it should be.” Home to more than 50 wineries, the region is a community that is resurrecting true wine hospitality.

The next time you are in Livermore Valley, I suggest driving on Tesla Road to the highest point, in the middle of the valley. Step out of your car and look out at the vast expanse of the vineyard land, olive trees, and small estates. Smell the sea breeze and take in the 360-degree view. Come frolic in Livermore Valley, where everyone knows your name. The best is yet to come, and we are here for it.

title: Sicily, Land of Unmatched Hospitality, Is the International Wine Region of the Year
summary:
Sicily has a winemaking tradition spanning at least 27 centuries and 17 civilizations, and its wines have never been better.

The post Sicily, Land of Unmatched Hospitality, Is the International Wine Region of the Year appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
When asked to describe, in three words, what makes Sicily a special winemaking region, President of the Consorzio di Tutela Vini DOC Sicilia Alessio Planeta responds: “history, biodiversity, and geodiversity.” But it’s too hard to choose just three, so he insists on adding another: “hospitality.” 

His struggle is understandable. The impossibility of explaining Sicily—of representing just how extraordinary it is, of communicating all the things it has been and might be—is perhaps its only definitional characteristic. 

Wine has been made in Sicily for at least 27 centuries by at least 17 different civilizations. Sicilia DOC wines can be produced from more than a dozen different indigenous grapes, with more than 50 rediscovered heritage varietals slowly coming into the fold, not to mention the many international varietals that also flourish here. They grow in soils that range from shimmering white calcareous and limestone near the Baroque city of Noto to pitch-black volcanic on Etna. The vines here confront climates that demand harvest in the steaming July heat in Trapani and deep into October on the peaks of the Sicani and Hyblaean mountains.

But the reason why Sicilia DOC wines shine so bright is that fourth element: hospitality. Not just because Sicilians themselves are so warm and welcoming, but because the glasses they pour at their tables mingle must and memories. Through their wines, Sicilians invite people to become a part of their island and its history, beckoning them to traverse territory that has at some point hosted nearly every Mediterranean culture, and many beyond. 

Planeta aspires to share this with many more people during his tenure as president; his dream is that “the incredible power of the word Sicily will be ever more linked to the wines that we produce here.”

People often say Sicily isn’t an island but rather a continent unto itself. This year, it is a Wine Star, but we might better say that Sicilia DOC wines are an entire constellation. The light they emit arrives from the distant past, illuminating a path ahead with a burning energy that has been present since before we counted time.

title: Everyone Is Freaking Out About El Niño—Except California Winemakers
summary:
They all love rain, and an early harvest means vintners are better prepared for a wet winter than ever.

The post Everyone Is Freaking Out About El Niño—Except California Winemakers appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Key Points

  • While officials fear California’s expected “super” El Niño, vintners eagerly welcome the rain to replenish vital water sources.
  • An exceptionally early harvest allowed winemakers time to prep fields with cover crops to prevent severe soil erosion.
  • Vintners remain cautious, hoping for manageable rainfall rather than destructive warm rain or atmospheric rivers.

Though no one knows for sure what will happen this winter when the “super” El Niño comes to shore, more people than ever are worrying about the weather pattern, which is expected to deliver major downpours to California due to a warmer-than-normal Pacific Ocean. 

With water temperatures reaching all-time highs, many Golden State municipalities are warning residents to prepare for flooding as public informational sessions overflow with concerned citizens. Governor Gavin Newsom even declared a state of emergency last month, before a single drop of rain fell.  

And yet vintners, whose livelihoods depend entirely on the weather, aren’t really freaking out at all. Indeed, many are downright excited for El Niño, which would recharge water sources, rinse the soil of built-up minerals, and nourish the vines for the next year, or years, to come.  

“Essentially, it’s rain,” says Jordan Lonborg, who works on properties across the Central Coast for Coastal Vineyard Care Associates. “We want it.” 

In other words? “That’s money in the bank,” said David Gates, who has run farming operations for Ridge Vineyards since 1989, regularly monitoring properties from Paso Robles and the Santa Cruz Mountains up to Sonoma and Mendocino. “It’s easier to cut leaves off vines,” he says of the vigor that a wet winter would trigger. “It’s harder to glue them on.”

In fact, due to the historically early harvest, which started in July and was mostly wrapped by early October, vineyards are better prepared for a wet winter than usual.

“One of the benefits of the early harvest is that we are already starting to get the vineyard prepped for winter in September,” says Nathan Kandler of Thomas Fogarty Vineyard, located atop the Santa Cruz Mountains. “When we’re picking until November, it’s hard to start prepping.”

He’s already spread most of his compost and cover crop seeds, whose growing roots protect the soil from erosion. Much of these efforts are paid for by grants from the San Mateo County’s Resource Conservation District. “We’re taking advantage of that to get things dialed,” he says. 

Preparing the Vineyards

Up in Napa County, there are strict guidelines and hard deadlines for controlling erosion based on the severity of slopes and the specific watersheds where vineyards are located. 

“These rules are in place because of experiences we had in the past,” says Jessica Luke Baumgartner, who manages 700 acres of vineyard for Cakebread Cellars. “As my grandmother says, don’t go around the same mountain twice.”

She’s already sent out all of her cover crop seeds, and is stockpiling straw wattles and hay bales just in case. “We’re just being extra diligent right now because we know it can be significant,” she says. “We can’t just take the chance.”

Baumgartner has seen both extremes, from drought years when the reservoirs were empty to stormy winters that caused the Napa River and nearby creeks to overflow their banks. Her strategy is to stay vigilant.

“Everything can be so different than what you calculate and anticipate,” she says. “So it’s about being present and having boots on the ground.” 

Not all rain is the same, and these vintners will be watching to see which kinds of storms come first. “The first few rains are really important,” says Gates from Ridge. “If they’re gentle, the ground gets moist and then you get a nice ground cover up and out before you get that first big storm of the year.”

He says the worst years for farming, especially on hillsides, is when the first rain comes on the back of tropical systems called atmospheric rivers, formerly known as the Pineapple Express. 

“Bare soil in California can take up to two inches in 24 hours without really causing a lot of erosion,” says Gates. “But anything more than that, especially if you don’t have good groundcover or a solid base of weeds or roots, it can cause some issues.”

There can certainly be too much of a good thing, especially come spring if the rains keep coming. Gates remembers early in his career not being able to take a road from Napa to Sonoma. “It had flipped the asphalt into the vineyard downstream,” he recalls. “It was a mess.”  

Lonborg witnessed similar destruction during wet years in Paso Robles, but it is more common in newly planted vineyards or those that don’t use cover crops. That was the case a few years ago, when a two-year-old vineyard was hammered by rain. “In two weeks, I watched the entire hillside slip,” says Lonborg. “ All of his trellises washed down the hill. It was gnarly.”

He highly suggests that vintners seed their bare ground this year, even if they usually don’t. “If it’s as big a winter as they’re calling for, every piece of ground has its limit,” he says. “If you hit that limit and don’t have a lot of roots, it could be a serious problem for sure.”

A Reminder to Reinforce

In the Sierra Foothills, where the slopes tend to be quite dramatic, Ann Kraemer welcomes the rain as well. Her hillsides at Shake Ridge Ranch haven’t been tilled in years, so the soil beneath the vines is not in danger of washing away. She is taking the El Niño threat as motivation to reinforce some problematic gullies, but her concern is more about the predicted winery warmth rather than the rain. 

“What’s scary about it is warmer rain, so less snowpack,” says Kraemer, who started planting her 46 acres of vines in 2003 after decades of working with big names in Napa and Sonoma. “Snowpack is what charges our water table.”

That snowpack moderates the mountainous region’s weather as well. “When we have good snowpack, even though the days might be hot, you get this cold air coming off the mountains,” she says. “It has a lot to do with our diurnal shit.”

She does worry about wine regions recently scorched by wildfires, which could see mudslides. “I feel for anybody who has had a fire in the last few years,” she says. “You don’t have that soil protection.” 

Of course, California isn’t the only region tracking El Niño, which affects rainfall and temperatures around the world. Australia and South Africa might be hotter and drier than normal, adding to wildfire threats, while South America’s wine scene might get doused like California. Europe is a bit more variable—a wetter winter would be great for Mediterranean regions, while drier summers can reduce disease pressure in the continental areas.  

The Remaining Unknowns

“Variable” describes all of this weather forecasting. Despite the dire warnings coming to California, these vintners are experiencing a bit of storm-prediction fatigue, and will believe it when they see it. Some of the driest years in recent memory came during El Niños, for instance. And the wettest year for Paso Robles came during the 2022 to 2023 La Niña event, which is the cool-water-powered little sister to El Niño that’s supposed to be dry. 

“It started raining in November and didn’t stop till April,” recalls Lonborg, who worked for Tablas Creek Vineyard at the time, when culverts backed up with debris and roads blew out. “That winter is probably in the back of everyone’s minds.”

And the indications keep piling on, whether it’s from meteorologists with the top technology or generational wisdom out in the field. “What I’ve heard from old timers around here is that when your oak trees drop a lot of acorns, it will be a wet winter,” says Baumgartner from Cakebread. “I’m literally standing under a massive oak right now, and I’m surrounded by acorns.”

These California vintners hope that this El Niño is neither a disaster or a dud—that the rain does come, but in a manageable manner. 

“Wine country is gonna look so different this year, especially if the big rains come,” says Lonborg, whose Coastal Vineyard Care is seeding thousands of acres right now across the state. “These cover crops are so colorful. It’s gonna be a sight for sore eyes, not to mention all the benefits to soil health.”

The post Agave Wine 101: What to Know About Tequila’s Low-Key Cousin appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
At Bar Snack in Manhattan’s East Village, Can de la Calle agave wine pops up in multiple drinks on the menu: the cheeky Ménage-A-gavé, a spiked plum lemonade, a spicy margarita variation—all alongside mezcal and sparkling wine. 

“I love it,” says bar owner Iain Griffiths of agave wine. “It gives our margarita rounded corners, if you will,” lowering the alcohol in the drink while still adding “a great little whack of agave in there.”

So what is agave wine, exactly? In brief, it’s sap extracted from the heart of the blue agave plant—the same base ingredient as tequila—fermented with yeast and fortified with a small amount of an agave-based spirit (usually tequila) for stability. 

It traces its roots back to pulque, an ancient drink made by Mexico’s Aztecs, who fermented the sap of the agave plant (aguamiel) as a ritual and ceremonial drink. When the Spanish arrived in Mexico in the 1500s, they brought distillation equipment and took a liking to pulque. That’s most likely when agave “wine” was first fortified, akin to vermouth or Spain’s sherry. 

Some agave wines are also sweetened, flavored, or both. Unlike tequila or mezcal, agave wines are not required to be made in Mexico, but most of the quality stuff does come from there. (Of course, this makes sense given proximity to tequila, but with the rise of global agave spirits, it’s possible that might one day change.) 

While agave wine has been enjoyed in Mexico for centuries—where it is usually considered a rustic drink, Griffiths explains—it’s a relative newcomer to the United States.

The New ‘It’ Drink

Expect to see agave wine popping up more frequently, riding the wave of renewed interest in tequila, as well as the ever increasing demand for lower-abv options. (Most agave wines land in the 20 to 25% abv range, compared to the typical 40% range of agave spirits like mezcal and tequila.)

Food and drink trend forecaster Tastewise even declared it “the new ‘it drink,’” in its 2026 Food & Beverage Trend Forecast report, with a 73% year-over-year increase in the appearance of agave wine in menus.

“It’s taking a lot of the ground laid by tequila-based cocktails,” says Wesley Allan, an integrated marketing manager and consumer insights expert at Tastewise. “As a result of increasing prices and the rejection of overly flash tequila brands, we’ve found agave wine jumped to the fore.” In particular, he points to Rancho la Gloria, which specializes in flavored agave wine, as making headway at large restaurant chains in the United States.

Agave wine is particularly gaining ground in U.S. states with higher Mexican populations, who may already be familiar with the product. In particular, it has gained traction on menus in Texas, California, Florida (where the restaurant chain Tijuana Flats is one of the leaders using agave wine), Oregon, Utah, and New Mexico, Allan says. That’s followed by “a little bit of interest” in Louisiana, North Carolina, and South Carolina.

The Low-ABV Marg Has Entered the Chat

Agave wine, with its typically lower abv, also appeals to venues with beer and wine licenses who can’t serve hard liquor, and spots that deliberately curate low-alcohol drink menus. Sipeos, a Mediterranean restaurant in Walnut Creek, CA, fits both of those descriptions. And their low-abv margarita, made with Ola Sol agave wine, lime, and agave syrup, is their most popular cocktail.

“You really do taste the agave. It really shines through,” says bar manager Vincenzo Piccione, who also works agave wine into Paloma and Tequila Mule variations. Some guests even come in and request shots of the product, according to owner Hetal Shah: “It tastes like a tequila. It’s so close that it’s hard to tell unless you’re a tequila connoisseur.” 

Of note, not all agave wine is created equal. Traditionally, it’s been made with the runoff of mixto tequila—typically lower-quality tequila that contains non-agave sugar sources. 

Historically speaking, Griffiths explains, “agave wine is a very working class, lower socioeconomic drink.” A golden hue is often a giveaway that it’s made with mixto. However, some of the new-gen agave wines (and RTD beverages made with agave wine) have been made with an eye toward quality. See some of our recommendations below.

‘A Big Blank Canvas’

Is this agave wine’s moment? It certainly seems to fit the zeitgeist.

“I’m not surprised it’s trending,” Griffiths says. “It ticks so many wonderful boxes,” ranging from enthusiasm for agave spirits and lower-alcohol options to a new understanding that “not all sugar is bad for you, and sugar to add texture is good.” Indeed, agave wine’s lightly honeyed flavor profile adds to its appeal.

If anything is holding agave wine back, posits Allan of Tastewise, it’s a lack of understanding about the product, as well as state-by-state restrictions. “Sometimes it’s treated like a spirit, which has stricter regulations than a wine,” he explains. Amorphous rules around formulation and sourcing of agave as well as the current tariff situation also play a role.

Yet, the road ahead is potentially exciting.

“There’s a very big blank canvas sitting behind agave wine right now,” Griffiths suggests. Imagine the possibilities of a mezcal-fortified variation, or a terroir-focused agave wine, for example. “It will be exciting to see who runs with it, where they take it from here.”

Four Agave Wines to Try

Ola Sol Agave Wine ($27; 25% abv). Most likely to please fans of blanco tequila, this clear liquid has a crisp jalapeño pepper flavor and scent, finishing with white pepper sparks and a vegetal bell pepper exhale.

Can de la Calle Mexican Agave Wine ($21 for 1 liter; 24% abv). From Mally Barajas, a master distiller with La Gritona tequila, this is a mellow and mixable option. Expect a faint pale straw tinge and a lightly honeyed palate, finishing with a lingering dulce de leche note.

Rancho La Gloria Ready to Drink Margarita Wine Cocktail ($17; 13.9% abv). Made with “100% de agave wine” and real lime juice (and no mention of Mexico in the labeling), this sweet-tart marg has a pale yellow-green hue and pleasing lime flavor. While it lacks the agave punch of a true marg, it’s easy-drinking and as tasty as many RTDs on the market right now. 

Soula Agave Wine Margarita ($13 for 4-pack of 12-oz cans; 5% abv) Made with agave wine from Mexico, this launched in 2024. Founded by two women, Anita Goodson (who drew on her Mexican heritage for the RTD cocktail) and Melanie Nelson, these canned RTDs come in Mango Citrus, Lime, Paloma, and Pineapple Chili flavors.

title: The Most Bizarre Tale in the History of Oregon Wine
summary:
If you think the Rajneeshees were a bunch of counter-culture types who renounced all worldly pursuits, think again.

The post The Most Bizarre Tale in the History of Oregon Wine appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
I thought I knew all of Oregon’s best wine stories. I missed the one about the Indian guru who nearly launched a winery before his utopian community collapsed.

Bhagwan Shree Rajneesh, a.k.a. Osho, came to the United States in January 1981, ostensibly seeking medical treatment for back pain. His move may have also been due to tax issues with the Indian government and the need to find more space for his growing number of followers.

Six months later, Bhagwan’s personal secretary, Ma Anand Sheela, orchestrated the purchase of 64,229 acres of remote, highdesert land in Oregon’s Wasco County.

As any good guru does, Bhagwan had amassed a large group of devotees. They worked long hours to transform the area locals called the Big Muddy Ranch into an incorporated city named Rajneeshpuram. Eventually, they would also annex the neighboring town of Antelope—a move that did not sit well with its 40 residents

Thanks to attempted political assassinations, arson, a bioterror attack, immigration-fraud charges, and other legal troubles, the Rajneeshpuram experiment came to a screeching halt at the end of 1985 amid allegations of child abuse at the commune.

Cut to 2021, when I finally got around to binge-watching Wild, Wild Country, the Netflix docuseries about Rajneeshpuram. It inspired me to pick up a copy of historian Frances FitzGerald’s book, Cities on a Hill: A Journey Through Contemporary American Cultures. In the chapter on Rajneeshpuram, FitzGerald wrote, “Since July of 1981, the Rajneeshee had—they said—cleared 3,000 acres of land and planted them with winter wheat, sunflowers, vegetables, vines, and fruit trees.”

Vines? I’ve been covering Oregon wine for decades. How did I not know about this? I had a lot of questions.

The Search for Answers

My investigation began with an artist named Rashid Maxwell, known in his Rajneesh days as Swami Deva Rashid. Rashid worked in agriculture at Rajneeshpuram, so I hoped he could shed some light on these mysterious vines. He said he didn’t spend much time in the vineyard and pointed me toward Swami Veet Chintan, who was responsible for planting Rajneeshpuram’s grapevines. Chintan was happy to share all the vineyard details through a series of phone calls and emails from his home in Slovenia.

Chintan brought a good deal of expertise to Rajneeshpuram when he arrived in July 1981. He earned a master’s degree in agriculture in Switzerland, studying viticulture and winemaking. At Rajneeshpuram, he helped establish a dairy farm named Rabiya. He traveled to Washington State to purchase cuttings for the commune’s vineyard, but came home empty-handed due to the red tape involved with transporting vine cuttings across state lines.

So Chintan headed to the Willamette Valley and successfully sourced cuttings from a nursery. I suspected it was Dick Erath’s famed nursery, but he said he wasn’t sure. In the fall of 1982, Chintan helped plant 12,500 Chardonnay, Riesling, Gewürztraminer, Pinot Noir, and table grape vines in Rajneeshpuram’s nineacre vineyard.

“I remember that we planted the vines with six feet between rows and four feet between vines along one row,” Chintan said. Backed by rock-strewn slopes and dramatic cliff walls, the southward-facing vineyard sat at an elevation of 1,420 to 1,480 feet.

Did the vineyard have a name? Chintan said he didn’t know of any, but added that, “I’m sure someone in one of our departments had a name in mind.”

The vineyard’s location was remote, even by Rajneeshpuram standards. “Not many people knew what we were doing out there,” Chintan said.

He worked closely with Rajneeshpuram’s farm coordinator, an Australian named Swami Anand Neehar. “It was a team effort, where I would help with pruning the vines and checking the irrigation, but I was mostly consulting with Neehar and supervising others,” Chintan said.

A sophisticated Israeli drip irrigation system supplied water to the vineyard. This system predated Argyle Winery’s pioneering irrigation efforts in the Willamette Valley, which started in 1988.

By 1983, grapes began appearing on the vines that Chintan and Neehar had shepherded from infancy. Those first grapes made their way to Magdalena, the commune’s 10,000-square-foot cafeteria and bakery.

Disaster struck the next winter when temperatures in the vineyard dropped to 30 degrees below zero. Chintan supervised the cutting back of the vines, which basically meant starting over.

After a small harvest in 1984, fruit production ramped up in 1985. The wine writer James Conaway toured Rajneeshpuram with Neehar that summer. Conaway described the visit for an article in the academic journal The Hedgehog Review: “He is taking me on a tour in his pickup, past the dairy barn, fields redolent of irrigation sewage, and a vineyard expected to produce 14 tons of grapes that Bhagwan intended to turn into a distinguished wine.”

That “distinguished wine” wasn’t going to be limited to on-commune consumption. “We absolutely planned to make wine commercially,” Chintan told me. Neehar boldly predicted they would make 16,000 bottles of wine in 1986.

The name “Wasco White” was jokingly suggested for one of the wines, a nod to the county where Rajneeshpuram was located. One vineyard worker told a reporter for The Rajneesh Times, Rajneeshpuram’s paper of record, that “Chateau Rajneesh” had a nice ring to it.

Swami Prartho Subhan, an attorney and avid wine buff, brought wine to the commune from Baltimore. At one tasting Subhan hosted, he poured a 1970 Beaulieu Vineyards Georges de Latour Private Reserve Cabernet Sauvignon for his friends in Rajneeshpuram. It did not surprise me at all to learn that Subhan had tasted wine back home in Maryland with another attorney, Robert M. Parker, Jr.

Wine tastings were held every Wednesday evening inside a deli called Zorba the Buddha Rajneesh. The deli was also a bottle shop with an Australian Shiraz-heavy inventory. The Rajneesh Times declared in a January 1985 article that “Rajneeshpuram is wine country,” noting that sales at the deli and the Zorba the Buddha Restaurant and Lounge were “brisk.”

With a population of around 2,000 people, having several Oregon Liquor Control Commission licenses to sell and pour wine, beer, and spirits was impressive. The Rajneeshees were hardly teetotalers. Subhan, who now runs a meditation center in Seattle, told me, “There’s so much more to Rajneeshpuram than what you saw in Wild, Wild Country.”

Work Hard, Shop Harder

If you think the Rajneeshees were a bunch of counter-culture types who renounced all worldly pursuits, think again. “We’re not hippies,” Sheela told a reporter for The Oregonian newspaper in January 1983. “Bhagwan teaches us the Rolls-Royce style. We’re a bunch of capitalists.”

The Rajneeshes coveted the lifestyle perks they had enjoyed before arriving in rural Oregon, and Devarteerth Mall was where they could indulge their material desires. Like any good 1980s mall, Devarteerth offered several places to eat, a clothing boutique, a beauty parlor, and a stereo store. At the Omar Khayyam Lounge and Cardroom, guests could quaff alcoholic beverages while boogieing to “It’s Raining Men” by The Weather Girls.

My favorite discovery, however, was that The Rajneesh Times had an excellent weekly wine column. The columnist was Swami Shanti Prabhu, also known as Tim McCarthy, who died in 2021. His brother, Dano McCarthy, told me that Prabhu likely picked up his expertise while working in sales for a wine distributor. One week, Prabhu would recommend an obscure sparkling wine from Côtes du Rhône, and the next week he would be off in the Jura region or recommending a Grignolino from Piedmont. Few wine columns in early-1980s American newspapers covered this much ground.

There was clearly a lot of interest in wine in Rajneeshpuram, but by the time Chintan was ready to start making some in 1985, there was no money left for equipment. “After all the work that we did to keep that vineyard going, it was incredibly disappointing,” Chintan said.

It is hard to resist daydreaming about what might have been if Rajneeshpuram had survived. Free labor, vineyard expertise, and good equipment would have been quite the competitive advantage in the Oregon wine market.

Fortunately, we have a document that gives us a glimpse of that future: the “City of Rajneeshpuram Comprehensive Plan.” Rajneeshpuram’s City Council described it as the “official guide for its future development.” The plan describes building a small winery to “produce Eastern Oregon rosé and white wines.” The Rajneeshees also hoped to expand their vineyard to 30 acres. After assessing the local climate, the document predicts growing more than three to four tons of grapes per acre and producing more than 2,000 bottles per acre. That would have been a lot of wine by 1980s Oregon standards.

Caller on the Line

For me, the most surreal part of this story occurred during Thanksgiving dinner with my family in 2021. That’s when Sheela called me. Sheela was Bhagwan’s right hand, the often-strident spokesperson whom Oregonians frequently saw in segments about the commune on local news.

I had left a phone message and sent an email to the nursing-home business Sheela operated in Switzerland. I never in a million years thought that she would respond.

Sheela was polite and charming on the phone, but she didn’t remember much about Rajneeshpuram’s wine culture, and only vaguely remembered people planting grapes. She claimed that she had her mind on “more important things” at the time. I asked Sheela if she had any favorite wines, Oregon or otherwise. She said that she was surrounded by good Swiss wines where she lived in the village of Maisprach. It was hard to reconcile the sweet voice on the other end of the phone with Sheela’s criminal convictions in the United States. But it did get me thinking: Given all of the terrible things that occurred at Rajneeshpuram, was I wrong to write an article about something so frivolous as the commune’s wine?

I asked Dickon Kent, who lived in Rajneeshpuram as a young boy, if I should proceed. Kent had been instrumental in connecting me with people who had lived in Rajneeshpuram.

“Why not?” Kent replied. “I think it’s good to celebrate the good and the bad that happened. And that’s coming from somebody who was just featured in a documentary about the child abuse at Rajneeshpuram. I think it’s the big piece that a lot of people seem to miss—there is light and dark to everything, and if we’re not willing to acknowledge them both, we’re missing half the story.”

The other half of the story is the stuff of daydreams, even if they went unfulfilled. A Rajneeshee winery would have benefited from low overhead and, thanks to its commercial baked goods and produce operations, a distribution network that ran all the way to Portland. Who knows, Chateau Rajneesh might have gone on to become an Oregon cult classic.

content:
Pennsylvania’s Underrated Wine Country Is Finally Getting Its Due

On a warm summer evening, I sit, wine glass in hand, watching the sunset over rows of verdant vines. As I slowly sip the easy-drinking Pinot Gris, I can feel my stress melt away.

Just two hours earlier, I was sitting in my tiny corner New York City work cubicle, under the glare of harsh overhead lights, fraught with worry, hastily trying to execute some tasks that, then, seemed vitally important. 

But, as I listen to the soft hum of crickets, I distinctly feel the environment shift my state of mind. I am in my happy place: wine country. Best of all? It’s just a quick drive away in Pennsylvania.

A year prior to this visit, an email popped up in my inbox inviting me on an excursion to some wineries in Pennsylvania. My initial response was one of bewilderment. But my curiosity kicked in. I began Googling images of Pennsylvania wine country, and came upon picture after picture of a growing farm and wine community.

Pennsylvania, as a wine region, had seedlings in the 17th century when William Penn planted the first vineyard in 1683. To put this in a broader perspective, around this same time Bordeaux had just drained its marshes to expand its winegrape plantings. Its global acclaim was just starting to take root.

A Place in American Wine History

In fact, America’s first commercial vineyard was founded in 1787—in Pennsylvania. Its shareholders included such notable figures as Alexander Hamilton, Aaron Burr, and Johns Hopkins. This is some 50 years before George Yount christened a Napa vineyard.

The initial vine cuttings that were brought to Pennsylvania were vinifera in origin, hailing from Bordeaux. These, however, struggled to survive, but native American species and the European grape vines cross-pollinated to naturally produce what is now known as America’s first hybrid grape, the Alexander grape. 

While the Alexander grape no longer thrives in Pennsylvania, other hybrid grapes developed to persevere in humid environments are a part of the wine industry today. These include Chambourcin, Vidal Blanc, Traminette, Seyval Blanc, and Cayuga White, to name a few. The ubiquitous vinifera grapes, Chardonnay and Merlot, persist, as well, along with less common Cabernet Franc, Riesling, Albariño, and even Grüner Veltliner.

Diverse Terroir and Grapes

There are five recognized American Viticultural Areas (AVAs) within the state. Each one is vastly different from the others. 

Lake Erie AVA is the most isolated and expansive, crossing the state borders of New York and Ohio in the upper western corner. It is a cool climate AVA and known for hybrid grapes, like Concord, Niagara, and Vidal Blanc, and cold-hardy vinifera grapes like Riesling. Around 80% of Pennsylvania’s grapes are grown in Lake Erie AVA (including table grapes). 

The other AVAs are somewhat clustered in the southeastern corner, although still bolstering each their own unique climate and landscape. Lehigh Valley AVA, near Allentown, is the most prominent of the lot, responsible for 15 to 20% of Pennsylvania’s wine production. While hybrid Chambourcin is the most widely grown grape there, Vidal Blanc and Cayuga are also common, along with several vinifera varietals including Riesling, Grüner Veltliner, Albariño, and Cabernet Franc.

A Pastoral Utopia

Pennsylvania’s agricultural prowess goes well beyond wine grapes—and is a huge draw for visitors.There are vast dairy, livestock, grain, and specialty crop industries that are flourishing. Pennsylvania is also the top producer of mushrooms nationally. According to the Philadelphia Inquirer, 64% of the nation’s mushrooms are produced in the state.

These artisanal products are sprinkled across the vast landscape alongside the wineries—and come together for great dining experiences.

In my travels to Pennsylvania, though, the most memorable part is always the people, the farmers and winemakers.

One thing I have noticed throughout my visits to the region is just how warm and generous the hospitality can be. There is something special about being welcomed with the time and attention to really experience a place rather than simply pass through it. That kind of unhurried hospitality can feel both coveted and fleeting, yet I have found it again and again throughout the region. It is part of what makes visiting here so memorable.

Of the over 300 wineries in the state, a majority are small, independent, and run by families. This intimacy crosses into the programming these wineries offer.  Alongside wine tastings and walking tours, it is not uncommon to encounter live weekend music concert series, painting classes, bingo game nights, and seafood boils. There is a creative, lively, and artisanal element to the Pennsylvania wine community that is surprising, unexpected, and genuine.

If you would have told me last summer when I received that first email, that I would find an idyllic wine country escape and retreat not even two hours southwest of my humble, bustling, New York City abode, I surely would have looked at you with great skepticism. But there is a bucolic wine excursion awaiting exploration. It is my hope that more take advantage of this latent treasure.

title: Savory Cocktails Are Having a Moment. Here Are 23 to Try.
summary:
If you like your martinis with more olive brine than vodka, you’ll love these savory cocktails.

The post Savory Cocktails Are Having a Moment. Here Are 23 to Try. appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
As we mature as drinkers, our palates evolve. That’s why, much like a favorite childhood candy, sweet concoctions may not hit the same way over time. They may taste more cloying or lacking in complexity, leaving us wondering what else is out there. Enter savory cocktails, which call on flavors from fish sauce to chili bitters to challenge palates and offer delicious alternatives to sugar-forward drinks. Bars across the country are getting in on the trend, introducing new offerings that go far beyond olive juice-splashed dirty martinis.

In recent years, pickles have taken the internet by storm in the form of martinis, shots, and Sauvignon Blanc. Dirty martinis have even made the jump from drinks to food, inspiring everything from a briny salad dressing to an olive-studded pasta. It points to the wider embrace of savory cocktail flavors, particularly in combinations outside the norm.

“I’ve noticed a larger trend of people asking for traditional cocktails to be less sweet,” says bartender Emily Holser, adding that she believes this can be a gateway to expanding one’s palate.

Interested in finding a savory cocktail that speaks to you? For all of the umami lovers out there, here are some of Wine Enthusiast’s favorite savory libations, from an everything bagel-inspired martini to a jerk spice daiquiri.

The Classics

Dirty Martini

Forget sugary Appletinis and fruit juice-spiked Mississippi bourbon punch. If your drink preferences skew more savory than sweet, the dirty martini belongs in your order queue. With a deep umami kick from a heavy-handed splash of salty olive brine, this cocktail has earned its honored spot in the cocktail canon.

Spicy Margarita

Whether you’re a lifelong spice fiend or simply looking to heat up your next happy hour, consider the spicy margarita. With cucumber and jalapeño, this recipe brings a savory punch to the classic agave cocktail.

Bloody Mary

With ingredients such as horseradish, tomato juice, and hot sauce, the Bloody Mary might be one of the most polarizing classic cocktails. If you’re a die-hard fan, add a few drops of Worcestershire sauce.

Traditional Michelada

If your guests crave a savory hop-tail, try this Mexican classic. The michelada melds a Bloody Mary with Mexican light-style ale, while its salted rim gives a small nod to the country’s other signature drink: the margarita.

Adventurous Riffs

Dirty Spritz

Originating from viral bouts around social media, the Dirty Spritz is well on its way to classic cocktail status. Drinkers love this lower-abv twist on a dirty martini that combines sparkling wine, olive brine, and sherry.

Pickle Martini

Dirty martini lovers, we present to you: the pickle martini. This salty riff takes the classic one step further with the addition of pickle brine, while aquavit adds an herbal touch.

Tomatini

Tomato cocktails have been making their way onto more and more menus in recent years with varying degrees of complexity. This tomatini recipe takes a simpler route by muddling a tomato with white balsamic vinegar, vodka, salt, and black pepper.

Jerk Daiquiri

Classic jerk seasoning highlights flavors such as hot peppers, thyme, and allspice. This jerk daiquiri infuses those flavors into the classic cocktail with a combination of thyme simple syrup, habanero smoked saline solution, and St. Elizabeth Allspice Dram.

Dill Breaker

While dill in a cocktail might have sounded insane a decade ago, it’s become much more palatable to modern tastes as savory cocktails have made their way mainstream. The Dill Breaker, which blends dill cordial with vodka and lemon juice, is actually one of the tamer drinks on this list.

Everything Bagel Martini

Building off classic dirty martini ingredients, this everything bagel martini just makes sense. Everything bagel spice delivers rich umami flavor and an appealingly crunchy texture—it’s our new favorite thing to put on a martini rim.

Mexican Martini

What do you get when you cross a dirty martini with a margarita? A Mexican martini, of course. Olive brine meets classic margarita ingredients in this savory riff, served up. If you want to add a salt rim, we wouldn’t be mad.

Smoky Mary

If you want to take your Bloody Mary to the next level, try the Smoky Mary. Mezcal imparts a savory, smoky note to the classic brunch cocktail.

Pickle Shot

This strong-and-sour pickle shooter has been making the rounds on social media for the past couple of years. We can see why: It’s a fun, playful drink that’s easy to make and adapts to whichever ingredients are in your bar/kitchen.

Crazy Concoctions

Chicken Soup Martini

Don’t worry, this chicken soup martini doesn’t actually contain any poultry. Rather, it relies on a combination of olive brine and a mirepoix infusion to channel all the savory, umami flavors.

Tomato-Anchovy Martini

Want to mix up something even crazier than a tomatini? Check out the tomato-anchovy martini. This drink uses Veso’s Anchovy Vermouth for a saline touch that isn’t too overpowering.

Parmesan Espresso Martini

Behold the parmesan espresso martini—which is exactly what it sounds like and better than you’d expect. The parmesan-infused vodka and thin layer of grated cheese make a delightfully smooth and savory cocktail.

Celine-Dijon

File this under unlikely combinations that somehow just work. The pun-tastic Celine-Dijon, which gets its punch from Dijon mustard and passionfruit, makes our heart go on.

Latke Sour

With a spuds-forward flavor, rich froth, and a whiff of smokiness, the Latke Sour is practically a potato pancake in drink form.

Seven Serpents

Taking inspiration from the Aztec goddess of corn and sustenance, Chicomecóatl, the Seven Serpents is a spicy corn cocktail featuring chili bitters, fresh corn juice, lemon juice, and the spirit of your choice.

Smoke on the Water

Yes, making the nori-infused gin for the Smoke on the Water requires a little bit of planning, but once that’s done, it’s smooth sailing ahead. The addition of white port and Talisker make up this smoky yet salty cocktail.

Sober Sippers

Non-Alcoholic Bloody Mary

One could argue that this non-alcoholic Bloody Mary is just gazpacho in a glass, but we like to think this batched mocktail is more than that. If you want to truly distinguish it, add your favorite NA spirit.

Non-Alcoholic Michelada

This NA Michelada is perfect when entertaining teetotalers and drinkers alike. Simply prepare the savory accouterments and crack open a variety of alcoholic and non-alcoholic light beers.

Carrot Mocktail

With fresh orange juice and zero-proof tequila, this savory and sophisticated mocktail is worth sipping all year long.

title: This Internet-Famous Korean Coffee Drink Is Even Better as a Cocktail
summary:
With rum, Frangelico, and coconut soju, the Dalgona cocktail is a delightful sweet treat.

The post This Internet-Famous Korean Coffee Drink Is Even Better as a Cocktail appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
First, there was dalgona candy, a traditional Korean confection with flavors some liken to honeycomb or butterscotch; the word “dalgona” comes from the Korean word for “sweet.

Then came dalgona coffee, a popular Korean coffee drink that went viral on social media in 2020. It seemed like everyone was vigorously mixing instant coffee, sugar, and hot water until thick, caramel-colored peaks emerged. The fluffy, toffee-like cloud was then spooned atop milk for a sweet, drinkable treat.

This next creative evolution is a mash-up of dalgona coffee and the espresso martini, courtesy of Haera Shin, the beverage director for Momofuku, David Chang’s restaurant group. A native New Yorker with Korean heritage, Shin was inspired by the series Squid Game to make this playful riff, which was on the menu at the Netflix Bites pop-up restaurant in Las Vegas. The recipe is also featured in her new book, Korean Cocktails: From Traditional Spirits to Modern Drinks.

“In the first season [of Squid Game], one of the challenges involves carving out a shape from a dalgona candy,” she recalls. The South Korean survival drama debuted in 2021—right around the height of the global dalgona coffee craze.

Instead of vodka, flavored soju adds a focused burst of coconut flavor alongside rum, while a frothy Korean coffee whip evokes the popular caffeinated quaff.

“Don’t worry,” Shin assures. “No deadly consequences if you fail this challenge!”

Dalgona

Courtesy of Korean Cocktails: From Traditional Spirits to Modern Drinks by Haera Shin (Countryman Press, 2026)

Ingredients

1 ½ ounces Planteray Rum 3 Stars (or other preferred white rum)
¾ ounce Frangelico
½ ounce coconut soju
2 ounces oat milk
½ ounce honey syrup (1:1 honey to water)
Whipped Korean coffee, to top*

Directions

Combine all ingredients except whipped coffee in a cocktail shaker with ice. Shake vigorously, then strain into a snifter filled with ice. Spoon whipped coffee on top.

*To make whipped Korean coffee: Combine ¼ cup instant coffee, ¼ cup boiling water, and ¼ cup sugar in a medium bowl. Whip together with a handheld mixer until light and fluffy, with medium-stiff peaks. Store in a container in the refrigerator until ready to use, for up to one day. Makes ½ cup whipped cream (enough for 2 drinks).

title: A Promising New AVA Is Gaining Traction in the South
summary:
Despite just being established in 2025, North Carolina’s Tryon Foothills AVA is already making a name for itself.

The post A Promising New AVA Is Gaining Traction in the South appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Michael Myers, the executive beverage director for Charlotte, North Carolina’s Irreverently Refined hospitality group, knows a lot about wine. But when he needed to find local wines for a special North Carolina-themed menu at one of his restaurants, he wasn’t sure where to look.

“North Carolina wines weren’t really on our list,” Myers says. “We had maybe used one or two. And it kind of started as a joke: ‘What are we going to use for North Carolina wine?’ No one wanted to force it and just use North Carolina wines because we had to.”

But when Myers tasted a couple of wines from the nearby Tryon Foothills AVA, about 90 minutes west of Charlotte, he changed his mind.

“It was one of the most humbling things for me as a wine person that I didn’t know about these wines,” he says. “They were in my backyard.”

In many of the United States’s smaller, less-known American Viticultural Areas—and especially those that aren’t on the West Coast—this isn’t unusual. In North Carolina, the conversation usually begins and ends with the 150,000-case winery at the historic Biltmore Estate in Asheville.

YEAR AVA ESTABLISHED: 2025
TOTAL ACREAGE: 112,512
PLANTED ACREAGE: 50
NUMBER OF WINERIES: 4 ELEVATION RANGE: 712 to 1,656 feet

In this case, though, Tryon Foothills, despite being one of the country’s newest AVAs and having only a handful of wineries, has garnered more attention than its youth and production size would seem to warrant.

“We use it as a talking point, as a teaching point, about what can be done with an AVA,” says Nicole Chesney, the executive director of the North Carolina Wine & Grape Council. “It’s really been fun to see what has been done in the AVA.”

The Tryon Foothills AVA was only established in September 2025, but grape cultivation in the area dates back at least 150 years, including Muscadines. The region sits on the eastern foothills of the Blue Ridge Mountains, reaching elevations of up to 1,600 feet. That accounts for the unique feature in its terroir that justified the creation of the AVA—a “thermal belt,” where warm air remains on the slopes while cooler air drains to the valley floors below, creating a grape-growing environment that is much different from elsewhere in the state.

Tryon Hills doesn’t have the humidity or heat problems found elsewhere in North Carolina that require growers to focus on hybrid grapes. Rather, it allows them to work with more vinifera, like Merlot and Petit Verdot, says Cory Lillberg, the vineyard manager at Parker-Binns Vineyard. He was also the driving force behind the AVA petition, which had been lingering for almost two decades.

Lillberg says vinifera in the Tryon Foothills can ripen and hang longer, resulting in higher alcohol levels and wines that are richer and fruitier than those from other parts of the state and across much of the East Coast.

“The geologic conditions really give us a style and expression that’s different,” says Lillberg, whose winery makes between 3,000 and 5,000 cases a year.

The next goal? To attract more wineries and growers to take advantage of that unique terroir—which Lillberg hopes the new AVA will help accomplish.

MOST WIDELY PLANTED GRAPES: Merlot, Petit Verdot, Vidal Blanc, Petit Manseng
CLIMATE: Moderate, with an occasional early frost
SOIL TYPES: Rocky, clay, and loam

Bet You Didn’t Know

From the late 19th century until World War II, Tryon’s Rockhouse Winery shipped its grapes—primarily Niagara and Delaware—around the U.S., and “Tryon and grapes were synonymous like Milwaukee and beer,” according to the book Tryon Memories by Elizabeth Doubleday Frost.

content:
The Dinner Party Is Dead. Let’s Have a Séance.

Those who feed the village also get to build it.

I cannot stop thinking about a recent article from The Atlantic titled “Why Americans Stopped Throwing Dinner Parties.” The statistics are staggering. From 1975 to 2026, the percentage of Americans who host friends or family at least once a month dropped from 42% to 12%. That’s a 70% decline in just over 50 years.

This cliff-like drop isn’t simply because people are going out more. Rather, it’s because eating and being alone is the easiest it’s ever been. .

People collectively say they want more time spent with their community, socializing, and being together. But when it comes to actually making it happen, gathering becomes another daunting task, one so easily avoided by staying home and scrolling through our personalized feeds.

It reminds me of an expression I keep seeing on social media, especially in conversations about parenting and community: Everyone wants a village, but nobody wants to be a villager.

As a busy parent living in a small community, I resonate with this sentiment deeply. And perhaps nowhere is it felt more acutely than among parents of young children. The Atlantic article cites how much more time parents spend with their kids than at any other point in recent history. We’re more involved, more scheduled, and more exhausted with family life, and with that more isolated from our larger support networks.

But here’s the thing about a village: It doesn’t build itself. Someone has to invite the townspeople over. Someone has to put food on the table. Someone has to be willing to make the effort, even when it’s inconvenient.

Of course there’s the argument that hosting is a luxury. And sure, it can be. But I can tell you firsthand that the bar is so low these days, simply letting people into your home and putting out whatever leftovers, random snacks, or open bottle of wine is in your fridge is more than enough. 

My grandma, a devoted student of the Depression era, living off practically nothing, used to always say, “Even if we only have tuna fish, at least we will be together.” That’s the sentiment we need to bring back. And I think the wine world is just the community to do it.

I’m not saying that simply because wine itself is the ultimate vehicle for gathering. I’m talking about the art of hospitality. The instinct to welcome people in, make them comfortable, feed them, pour them something delicious, and create an experience to remember, regardless of how much or little time it takes to prepare.

Social media hasn’t just forced us all into splintered isolation. It’s also raised the expectations of what it means to host. Every dinner party seems to require an impossibly beautiful tablesetting, elaborate menu, perfect lighting, and flowers that look like they were arranged by a professional. This barrier to entry is terrifying to newbies. I consider myself a very experienced host and even I can’t meet those expectations. 

But a dinner party doesn’t need to be a production to be meaningful.

When was the last time someone cooked dinner for you in their home? Really think about it. While I have high standards for my own cooking, even when I’ve just assembled what’s around to share, I have never had someone not be grateful. I often find myself throwing together a simple snack platter–olives, nuts, great butter with hunks of bread. Or if you’re feeling ambitious, some homemade hummus or this house-favorite scallion yogurt dip. The act itself feels more scarce than ever.

And let me tell you, as someone who’s become a very practiced host, the effort—no matter how large or small—will always pay you back in spades.

I’ve built new friendships, forged relationships, heard incredible gossip, and ended countless nights dancing in my kitchen while doing the dishes to early 2000s pop-punk. Was I tired the next day? Of course. But I’m tired all the time. I have two young kids and a demanding full time job, just like everyone else.

Yet, there’s something wonderful about that sleepy glow of exhaustion after a night spent bringing people together. It’s the kind of tiredness that feels like you actually did something worthwhile with your life.

We can’t keep wishing for deeper friendships, stronger neighborhoods, and a greater sense of belonging while waiting for someone else to organize it all. Being a good villager means showing up for other people. And in my opinion, being a host is a huge part of that.

Inconvenience is the cost of community. 

Which brings me back to the wine community.

We are surrounded by people who understand the magic of gathering around a table. People who know that a bottle of wine tastes better when it’s shared, that food doesn’t need to be fancy to be memorable, and that hospitality is about how you make people feel, not how impressive your house looks. You know the junk drawer? I have junk tablescapes. 

We have the knowledge, the instincts, and the passion to make hosting feel accessible again. So why aren’t we teaching more people how to do it?

Here’s my conch call to all the hospitality folks out there in the wine community: We need you more than ever.

Help me bring back the dinner party. Even a lingering lunch will do. Not the intimidating, Instagram-perfect version. The real one. The one where the kitchen sink is full of dishes, someone’s sitting next to a cutting board on the counter, the food is simple, and nobody wants to leave. 

Let’s teach people how to host without making it a monumental undertaking. Dinner Party 101. The absolute laziest way to throw a great party. What to cook, what to pour, what to skip, and how to stop worrying about whether everything is perfect.

This is why we launched a Home & Entertaining section of the site dedicated to highlighting all the ways people gather, including how well-known hosts like Vin et Hip Hop founder Jermaine Stone and lifestyle influencer Chloe Crane-Leroux throw a party, to wine recommendations for hosting a low-key girls night in.

Because everyone wants a village. It’s time we all started acting like villagers. And if all we have is tuna fish and a bottle of wine, at least we’ll be together. I’ll bring the can opener and the corkscrew. 

Send me your best ideas, shortcuts, and hosting tricks, and I’ll start sharing them. Email me at jstrum@wineenthusiast.com or DM me @jackistrum. 

Jacqueline Strum

title: Livermore Valley, American Wine Region of the Year, Is Making Wine Joyful
summary:
The Livermore Valley has always been one of the hallmark regions for winemaking in Northern California. But its collaborative spirit is fueling an even brighter future.

The post Livermore Valley, American Wine Region of the Year, Is Making Wine Joyful appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Livermore Valley, California, is being recognized as Wine Enthusiast’s 2026 American Wine Region of the Year. But what makes this year different from any other?

The Livermore Valley has always been one of the hallmark regions for grape-growing and winemaking in Northern California. In addition to winning the Grand Prize at the Paris Exposition in 1889, it’s responsible for one of the most phenomenal clonal selections of all time: the Wente Clone, which is used to make Chardonnay all over the world. 

Known for signature expressions of Sauvignon Blanc and Cabernet Franc, long-standing, multi-generational wineries (like Wente Family Vineyards and Concannon Vineyard) have continued to propel the region forward, while small family operations are experimenting with lesser-used varietals, like Torrontés and Timorasso. 

The Livermore Valley Wine Community has been run by Executive Director Brandi Lombardi for 19 years, and is the headquarters of the nearly two-year-old Global Artisan Vintners Alliance. The Global AVA is comprised of 12 wine regions around the world, including Livermore, and focuses on creating a “thriving and inclusive global wine economy that strengthens locally owned and operated wineries and fosters enhanced agritourism in lesser-known wine regions.”

In addition to tech-fueled population growth in the region, there has been a recent explosion of thoughtful wine events, including TASTE: The Livermore Valley Wine Experience, Terroir at the Table, and Cab Franc-A-Palooza.

The region also has one of the highest percentages of women winemakers in the United States. The region’s mission has always reflected the Livermore Valley Wine Community’s tagline: “Wine tasting as it should be.” Home to more than 50 wineries, the region is a community that is resurrecting true wine hospitality.

The next time you are in Livermore Valley, I suggest driving on Tesla Road to the highest point, in the middle of the valley. Step out of your car and look out at the vast expanse of the vineyard land, olive trees, and small estates. Smell the sea breeze and take in the 360-degree view. Come frolic in Livermore Valley, where everyone knows your name. The best is yet to come, and we are here for it.
