title: Sicily, Land of Unmatched Hospitality, Is the International Wine Region of the Year
summary:
Sicily has a winemaking tradition spanning at least 27 centuries and 17 civilizations, and its wines have never been better.

The post Sicily, Land of Unmatched Hospitality, Is the International Wine Region of the Year appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
When asked to describe, in three words, what makes Sicily a special winemaking region, President of the Consorzio di Tutela Vini DOC Sicilia Alessio Planeta responds: “history, biodiversity, and geodiversity.” But it’s too hard to choose just three, so he insists on adding another: “hospitality.” 

His struggle is understandable. The impossibility of explaining Sicily—of representing just how extraordinary it is, of communicating all the things it has been and might be—is perhaps its only definitional characteristic. 

Wine has been made in Sicily for at least 27 centuries by at least 17 different civilizations. Sicilia DOC wines can be produced from more than a dozen different indigenous grapes, with more than 50 rediscovered heritage varietals slowly coming into the fold, not to mention the many international varietals that also flourish here. They grow in soils that range from shimmering white calcareous and limestone near the Baroque city of Noto to pitch-black volcanic on Etna. The vines here confront climates that demand harvest in the steaming July heat in Trapani and deep into October on the peaks of the Sicani and Hyblaean mountains.

But the reason why Sicilia DOC wines shine so bright is that fourth element: hospitality. Not just because Sicilians themselves are so warm and welcoming, but because the glasses they pour at their tables mingle must and memories. Through their wines, Sicilians invite people to become a part of their island and its history, beckoning them to traverse territory that has at some point hosted nearly every Mediterranean culture, and many beyond. 

Planeta aspires to share this with many more people during his tenure as president; his dream is that “the incredible power of the word Sicily will be ever more linked to the wines that we produce here.”

People often say Sicily isn’t an island but rather a continent unto itself. This year, it is a Wine Star, but we might better say that Sicilia DOC wines are an entire constellation. The light they emit arrives from the distant past, illuminating a path ahead with a burning energy that has been present since before we counted time.

title: Everyone Is Freaking Out About El Niño—Except California Winemakers
summary:
They all love rain, and an early harvest means vintners are better prepared for a wet winter than ever.

The post Everyone Is Freaking Out About El Niño—Except California Winemakers appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Key Points

  • While officials fear California’s expected “super” El Niño, vintners eagerly welcome the rain to replenish vital water sources.
  • An exceptionally early harvest allowed winemakers time to prep fields with cover crops to prevent severe soil erosion.
  • Vintners remain cautious, hoping for manageable rainfall rather than destructive warm rain or atmospheric rivers.

Though no one knows for sure what will happen this winter when the “super” El Niño comes to shore, more people than ever are worrying about the weather pattern, which is expected to deliver major downpours to California due to a warmer-than-normal Pacific Ocean. 

With water temperatures reaching all-time highs, many Golden State municipalities are warning residents to prepare for flooding as public informational sessions overflow with concerned citizens. Governor Gavin Newsom even declared a state of emergency last month, before a single drop of rain fell.  

And yet vintners, whose livelihoods depend entirely on the weather, aren’t really freaking out at all. Indeed, many are downright excited for El Niño, which would recharge water sources, rinse the soil of built-up minerals, and nourish the vines for the next year, or years, to come.  

“Essentially, it’s rain,” says Jordan Lonborg, who works on properties across the Central Coast for Coastal Vineyard Care Associates. “We want it.” 

In other words? “That’s money in the bank,” said David Gates, who has run farming operations for Ridge Vineyards since 1989, regularly monitoring properties from Paso Robles and the Santa Cruz Mountains up to Sonoma and Mendocino. “It’s easier to cut leaves off vines,” he says of the vigor that a wet winter would trigger. “It’s harder to glue them on.”

In fact, due to the historically early harvest, which started in July and was mostly wrapped by early October, vineyards are better prepared for a wet winter than usual.

“One of the benefits of the early harvest is that we are already starting to get the vineyard prepped for winter in September,” says Nathan Kandler of Thomas Fogarty Vineyard, located atop the Santa Cruz Mountains. “When we’re picking until November, it’s hard to start prepping.”

He’s already spread most of his compost and cover crop seeds, whose growing roots protect the soil from erosion. Much of these efforts are paid for by grants from the San Mateo County’s Resource Conservation District. “We’re taking advantage of that to get things dialed,” he says. 

Preparing the Vineyards

Up in Napa County, there are strict guidelines and hard deadlines for controlling erosion based on the severity of slopes and the specific watersheds where vineyards are located. 

“These rules are in place because of experiences we had in the past,” says Jessica Luke Baumgartner, who manages 700 acres of vineyard for Cakebread Cellars. “As my grandmother says, don’t go around the same mountain twice.”

She’s already sent out all of her cover crop seeds, and is stockpiling straw wattles and hay bales just in case. “We’re just being extra diligent right now because we know it can be significant,” she says. “We can’t just take the chance.”

Baumgartner has seen both extremes, from drought years when the reservoirs were empty to stormy winters that caused the Napa River and nearby creeks to overflow their banks. Her strategy is to stay vigilant.

“Everything can be so different than what you calculate and anticipate,” she says. “So it’s about being present and having boots on the ground.” 

Not all rain is the same, and these vintners will be watching to see which kinds of storms come first. “The first few rains are really important,” says Gates from Ridge. “If they’re gentle, the ground gets moist and then you get a nice ground cover up and out before you get that first big storm of the year.”

He says the worst years for farming, especially on hillsides, is when the first rain comes on the back of tropical systems called atmospheric rivers, formerly known as the Pineapple Express. 

“Bare soil in California can take up to two inches in 24 hours without really causing a lot of erosion,” says Gates. “But anything more than that, especially if you don’t have good groundcover or a solid base of weeds or roots, it can cause some issues.”

There can certainly be too much of a good thing, especially come spring if the rains keep coming. Gates remembers early in his career not being able to take a road from Napa to Sonoma. “It had flipped the asphalt into the vineyard downstream,” he recalls. “It was a mess.”  

Lonborg witnessed similar destruction during wet years in Paso Robles, but it is more common in newly planted vineyards or those that don’t use cover crops. That was the case a few years ago, when a two-year-old vineyard was hammered by rain. “In two weeks, I watched the entire hillside slip,” says Lonborg. “ All of his trellises washed down the hill. It was gnarly.”

He highly suggests that vintners seed their bare ground this year, even if they usually don’t. “If it’s as big a winter as they’re calling for, every piece of ground has its limit,” he says. “If you hit that limit and don’t have a lot of roots, it could be a serious problem for sure.”

A Reminder to Reinforce

In the Sierra Foothills, where the slopes tend to be quite dramatic, Ann Kraemer welcomes the rain as well. Her hillsides at Shake Ridge Ranch haven’t been tilled in years, so the soil beneath the vines is not in danger of washing away. She is taking the El Niño threat as motivation to reinforce some problematic gullies, but her concern is more about the predicted winery warmth rather than the rain. 

“What’s scary about it is warmer rain, so less snowpack,” says Kraemer, who started planting her 46 acres of vines in 2003 after decades of working with big names in Napa and Sonoma. “Snowpack is what charges our water table.”

That snowpack moderates the mountainous region’s weather as well. “When we have good snowpack, even though the days might be hot, you get this cold air coming off the mountains,” she says. “It has a lot to do with our diurnal shit.”

She does worry about wine regions recently scorched by wildfires, which could see mudslides. “I feel for anybody who has had a fire in the last few years,” she says. “You don’t have that soil protection.” 

Of course, California isn’t the only region tracking El Niño, which affects rainfall and temperatures around the world. Australia and South Africa might be hotter and drier than normal, adding to wildfire threats, while South America’s wine scene might get doused like California. Europe is a bit more variable—a wetter winter would be great for Mediterranean regions, while drier summers can reduce disease pressure in the continental areas.  

The Remaining Unknowns

“Variable” describes all of this weather forecasting. Despite the dire warnings coming to California, these vintners are experiencing a bit of storm-prediction fatigue, and will believe it when they see it. Some of the driest years in recent memory came during El Niños, for instance. And the wettest year for Paso Robles came during the 2022 to 2023 La Niña event, which is the cool-water-powered little sister to El Niño that’s supposed to be dry. 

“It started raining in November and didn’t stop till April,” recalls Lonborg, who worked for Tablas Creek Vineyard at the time, when culverts backed up with debris and roads blew out. “That winter is probably in the back of everyone’s minds.”

And the indications keep piling on, whether it’s from meteorologists with the top technology or generational wisdom out in the field. “What I’ve heard from old timers around here is that when your oak trees drop a lot of acorns, it will be a wet winter,” says Baumgartner from Cakebread. “I’m literally standing under a massive oak right now, and I’m surrounded by acorns.”

These California vintners hope that this El Niño is neither a disaster or a dud—that the rain does come, but in a manageable manner. 

“Wine country is gonna look so different this year, especially if the big rains come,” says Lonborg, whose Coastal Vineyard Care is seeding thousands of acres right now across the state. “These cover crops are so colorful. It’s gonna be a sight for sore eyes, not to mention all the benefits to soil health.”
